newsitem.title: USA: Texaco reaches $176 mln settlement in race case.
newsitem.headline: Texaco reaches $176 mln settlement in race case.

text.p: Texaco Inc. said on Friday it reached a $176 million pact to settle a racial discrimination lawsuit filed against it by six black employees in 1994.
The plaintiffs' group, representing 1,400 black employees who joined the suit, said the settlement was the biggest in a racial discrimination case by a corporation in the United States.
The agreement, which must be approved by a federal court in New York, included $115 million in an immediate cash payment to the black employees who worked at the company from 1991 to the present.

It included $26 million in a roughly 10 percent salary increase over five years for current black employees, with the first raise effective January 1, 1997. In addition, the company agreed to spend $35 million to set up a task force to help improve the company's hiring and advancement of minorities.
The lawsuit charged the oil giant with systematically discriminating against blacks and denying them promotions.
"We have settled the case. We think it is precedent-setting," said Daniel Berger, one of the lawyers for the plaintiffs.

In a letter to employees announcing the settlement, Texaco Chairman Peter Bijur said Texaco would increase the amount of business it does with minority companies. This would include advertising, legal, banking, investment management and accounting firms.
He also said the company "will actively work to increase the number of Texaco-branded stations owned by minorities and women."
"I have committed myself -- and the entire management team of this company -- to the elimination of any trace of discrimination in Texaco," he said.

Three members of the task force would be appointed by the plaintiffs and three by Texaco, with the chair to be agreed by both sides. The company said it would also set up diversity, sensitivity and mentoring programmes.
"With this litigation behind us, we can now move forward on our broader, urgent mission to make Texaco a model of work place opportunity for all men and women," Bijur said.
Texaco also said it would consider nationwide posting of openings for more senior positions than are currently listed.

The 2 1/2-year-old lawsuit sparked an outcry and a federal criminal probe last week against the company when tapes filed in the case came to light, suggesting that Texaco officials had dicussed destroying evidence sought in the case.

Transcripts of the tape, later partially corrected, were laced with racial slurs, including "black jelly beans," which the plaintiffs said backed up their allegations that officials at the company had been hostile to them.
Civil rights leaders, led by Rev. Jesse Jackson, this week threatened to launch a boycott of Texaco products and to picket its service stations starting on Saturday.
"It took the combination of the lawsuit, the courage of he workers, the embarrassment of the tapes, and the boycott to shake the process," Jackson told reporters in Washington.
Jackson said the boycott was "still very much a threat" and that he would talk to civil rights leaders across the country to decide whether or not to go ahead with their protests.
"There are a range of economic opportunities in Texaco that have not been addressed in this suit," he said. "I hope in the next few days ... they will be addressed by the company."

He said civil rights leaders wanted to see the company outline goals and timetables for increasing opportunities for minority-based businesses, investing in minority funds, and boosting minority ownership of Texaco service stations.
Texaco stock fell from a peak of $107 on Oct. 21 as low as $97 on Nov. 4 after the revelation about the tapes. It gained $2.75 Friday to close at $101.125 on the New York Stock Exchange.
"It is positive for Texaco in that this moves the issue behind them," said Steven Pfeifer, an oil sector analyst at Paine Webber.

"Without the tapes we would possibly be looking at another two years because of all the Texaco manoeuvring," Bari Ellen Robert, a black senior financial analyst who works at Texaco's headquarters in White Plains, New York, said at a news conference in New York.
"The atmosphere at work was mixed, it was full of tension. But when people actually sat down and they heard the case it did a lot," Roberts said.
Attorneys said the plaintiffs were pleased with the outcome. "They're ecstatic, and they believe the era of the 'good old boy' network at Texaco is coming to an end," said attorney Cyrus Mehri.
